claims.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys containing Hf, Zr, or Ti are susceptible to oxygen-induced embrittlement.
Gas-atomized HfNbTaTiZr powder can be consolidated by SPS at 1300 °C and subsequently processed by HPT.
Hydride precursors facilitate decomposition and oxygen scavenging in Group-IV-containing refractory high-entropy alloys.
An oxygen content below 0.15 wt% is achievable before or during consolidation of gas-atomized HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal decomposition of hydrides under vacuum or inert gas releases hydrogen while minimizing oxygen uptake.
SPS at 1300–1400 °C, 50–80 MPa, and a 2–5 minute dwell is suitable for these alloys.
A heating rate above 100 °C/min and a 2–5 minute dwell suppress phase separation during SPS.
Post-consolidation HPT, extrusion, or other severe plastic deformation refines grains and homogenizes the microstructure.
Processing requires either vacuum below 10^-3 Pa or argon containing less than 1 ppm oxygen.
Hot deformation at 950–1100 °C and HPT above 2.5 GPa are appropriate post-consolidation conditions.
A cooling rate of approximately 300 °C/min can be applied after SPS.
Rapid cooling and configurational entropy stabilize a metastable single-phase BCC random solid solution.
Severe plastic deformation produces a sub-micron grain size below 0.5 μm.
The proposed BCC structure and refined grains prevent nucleation of brittle alpha-HCP and oxide phases.
Brittle alpha-HCP, HfO2, or TiO phases typically form when oxygen exceeds 0.8 wt%.
Severe plastic deformation generates a dislocation density above 5 × 10^14 m^-2.
Dislocation accumulation, Hall–Petch strengthening, and solid-solution hardening increase yield strength while inhibiting phase separation.
The adapted process will produce a bulk alloy with relative density above 99%, oxygen below 0.15 wt%, and a single-phase BCC microstructure.
The processed alloy will have yield strength above 1.0 GPa at 800 °C.
The adapted process will avoid catastrophic cracking and reduce brittleness relative to conventional powder metallurgy.
